specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper proposes supervising attention in an ANN-based event detection (ED) model by constructing gold attention targets from annotated event arguments (two strategies: S1 argument-only, S2 argument+neighbors via Gaussian) and adding an L2 attention-fit term to the classification loss. Experiments on ACE 2005 (529/30/40 split) show supervised-attention variants (ANN-S1, ANN-S2) substantially outperform an unsupervised-attention baseline (ANN), with ANN-S2 reporting the best F1 (71.7) vs listed prior best (70.7). Augmenting training with FrameNet-derived events yields modest recall and F1 gains. The manuscript provides architectural detail and several controlled comparisons (ANN, ANN-ENT, ANN-Gold1/2, ANN-S1/S2). Key evidential support exists in Tables 2–4 and in the construction of S1/S2 and joint loss. Major evidentiary gaps: statistical testing protocol (number of runs / variance) is under-specified, sensitivity to λ and S2 Gaussian params is not reported, FrameNet augmentation pipeline injects unquantified noise, and fairness/reproducibility of comparisons to prior work depends on matching preprocessing and scripts which are not fully detailed. The claim that unsupervised attention fails due to ACE sparsity is plausible and partially supported (ANN improvement after FrameNet augmentation) but not conclusively isolated from other modeling factors.
logical_argument_graph: A: Arguments (annotated in ACE) are informative for disambiguating triggers → motivates supervising attention to focus on arguments.
B: Construct gold attention vectors from arguments (S1, S2) → define attention supervision targets α*.
C: Add attention-fit loss D(θ) (L2) weighted by λ to classification loss J(θ) → joint objective J'(θ) to train ANN and attention.
D: Train models (ANN baseline unsupervised; ANN-S1/ANN-S2 supervised) on ACE 2005 split → measure P/R/F1.
E: Observed: ANN-S1/ANN-S2 outperform ANN and prior reported baselines (Table 3) → conclude supervised attention improves ED; S2 trades recall for precision vs S1.
F: Augmenting with FrameNet-derived events increases recall and modestly F1 (Table 4) → supports data-sparsity explanation for unsupervised attention shortfall.
G: Therefore, supervised attention using argument annotations mitigates sparsity and yields state-of-the-art ED performance on ACE 2005.

identified_claims.claim_text: Annotated event-argument information (arguments) provides significant clues that can improve event detection (trigger identification and classification) when used explicitly.
evidence: Example in Introduction: 'fired' disambiguated by argument 'former protege'.
ANN-Gold1/2 (oracle-attention from arguments) outperform ANN and ANN-ENT in Table 2 (as described in Section 4.2).
uncertainty_flags: Table 2 numbers are referenced but not fully reproduced inline; effect sizes and variance for gold-attention experiments are not shown.
Evidence is limited to ACE 2005; generalization to other corpora or domains not demonstrated.

identified_claims.claim_text: Supervising the attention mechanism with constructed gold attention vectors derived from annotated arguments improves event detection performance compared to unsupervised attention mechanisms.
evidence: Model: joint loss J'(θ) = J(θ) + λ D(θ) (Eqns 8–9).
Reported results in Table 3: ANN (73.2/57.9/64.6) vs ANN-S1 (81.4/62.4/70.8) and ANN-S2 (78.0/66.3/71.7).
uncertainty_flags: Reported improvements depend on λ settings (λ=1.0 for S1, λ=5.0 for S2) but sensitivity/sweeps over λ not shown.
Number of experimental repeats and variance not specified, so robustness of reported gains is uncertain.

identified_claims.claim_text: Two strategies to construct gold attention vectors are effective: S1 assigns full attention to annotated arguments only; S2 spreads attention to argument words plus neighboring words using a Gaussian weighting (window size 3, µ=0, σ=1). S2 yields higher recall and S1 higher precision.
evidence: Precise definitions of S1 and S2 in Section 3.2.2 with hyperparameters described.
Experimental results: ANN-S1 shows higher precision (81.4) but lower recall (62.4) vs ANN-S2 (P 78.0, R 66.3) in Table 3.
uncertainty_flags: Effect of varying µ, σ, or window size is untested; the precision/recall pattern could change under other parameterizations.
No per-class breakdowns or statistical test specifically contrasting S1 vs S2; observed differences may not be significant across runs.

identified_claims.claim_text: The proposed supervised-attention ED model (ANN-S2) outperforms prior reported state-of-the-art methods on the ACE 2005 benchmark (best F1 reported), with significance claimed (t-test p ≤ 0.05).
evidence: Table 3: ANN-S2 F1=71.7 which is higher than Liu FN-Based 2016 F1=70.7 and other listed baselines.
Text reporting a t-test (p ≤ 0.05) that 'indicates our method significantly outperforms all compared methods.'
uncertainty_flags: Prior-method numbers may come from papers with differing preprocessing or splits; manuscript states split choice but does not fully document exact preprocessing/evaluation scripts for precise parity.
t-test details (paired/unpaired, number of runs, sample of metric values used) are not specified, raising uncertainty about the validity of the significance claim.

identified_claims.claim_text: Augmenting ACE 2005 training data with events extracted from FrameNet increases recall and can improve overall F1 for both baseline and supervised-attention models.
evidence: Table 4: ANN F1 improves 64.6→66.2 with FrameNet; ANN-S2 improves 71.7→71.9 (recall increases shown: ANN 57.9→59.2; ANN-S2 66.3→67.5).
Processing described: map FrameNet frame elements to arguments and use RPI IE system for entities.
uncertainty_flags: FrameNet-derived data required automatic processing and entity labeling; noise introduced by this pipeline is not quantified.
Improvements for ANN-S2 are marginal (0.2 F1), and statistical significance for augmentation gains is not reported.

identified_claims.claim_label: unsupervised attention fails due to data sparsity
identified_claims.claim_text: Unsupervised attention mechanisms trained solely on ACE 2005 cannot learn precise attentions because ACE 2005 training data is too sparse; supervised attention mitigates this limitation.
evidence: ANN baseline (unsupervised attention) performs poorly (F1=64.6) relative to supervised variants.
ANN performance improves when augmented with FrameNet (F1 64.6→66.2), suggesting data quantity matters.
uncertainty_flags: Causal attribution is plausible but not isolated: poorer ANN performance could also stem from architecture choices, attention formulation, or hyperparameter settings.
No learning curve experiments (varying ACE sample sizes) or controlled tests (same architecture but more data) to conclusively prove sparsity is the primary cause.

strengths.title: Clear operationalization of attention supervision
strengths.description: The manuscript precisely defines two concrete strategies (S1, S2) for constructing gold attention vectors from annotated arguments and integrates them via an L2 attention loss into the training objective.
evidence: Section 3.2.2: explicit definitions of S1 and S2, gaussian parameters µ/σ/window.
Equation 8–9: joint loss J'(θ) = J(θ) + λ D(θ).

strengths.title: Controlled experimental contrasts
strengths.description: Authors compare unsupervised baseline (ANN), entity-focused baseline (ANN-ENT), oracle-attention systems (ANN-Gold1/2), and supervised-attention variants (ANN-S1/S2), which helps trace impact of argument supervision.
evidence: Section 4.2: list and description of ANN, ANN-ENT, ANN-Gold1/2.
Tables 2 (referenced) and 3: comparative performance summaries.

strengths.title: Empirical gains on standard benchmark
strengths.description: Supervised-attention models show substantial absolute improvements in F1 over the unsupervised-attention baseline on ACE 2005 and ANN-S2 reports higher F1 than several prior reported systems.
evidence: Table 3: ANN 64.6 F1 vs ANN-S2 71.7 F1; prior best listed 70.7.
Table 4: FrameNet augmentation raises recall and F1 in some configurations.

strengths.title: Practical augmentation exploration
strengths.description: The work tests augmentation using FrameNet-derived events following prior literature and reports how augmentation affects recall/precision in supervised and unsupervised models.
evidence: Section 4.4: description of mapping FrameNet frame elements to ACE arguments and use of RPI IE system.
Table 4 shows changes pre/post augmentation.

concerns.title: Under-specified statistical testing and variance reporting
concerns.description: The manuscript claims statistical significance (t-test p ≤ 0.05) but does not report number of independent runs, random seeds, variance (std. dev.), or whether tests are paired. This prevents assessing whether gains are robust or within experimental noise.
evidence: Section 4.3 states 'We also perform a t-test (p ≤ 0.05)' but gives no protocol details.
Prior reviewers and shared_analysis flagged missing runs/variance.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report results over multiple (≥5–10) random seeds for each model variant; include mean±std for P/R/F1 and specify whether t-tests are paired and which metric samples were used. If compute is limited, use bootstrap resampling over test-set predictions.

concerns.title: Insufficient ablation isolating attention supervision effect
concerns.description: While supervised-attention models outperform ANN, the experiments do not fully isolate whether gains come from attention supervision specifically versus other changed hyperparameters (e.g., λ, dropout) or implementation details.
evidence: ANN-S1/S2 use specific λ values (1.0 and 5.0) and other hyperparameters; sensitivity sweeps are not reported.
Shared_analysis and prior reviewers call for ablations (J vs D vs varying λ).
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Include ablation experiments: (a) λ=0 (already ANN), (b) vary λ across a grid for S1/S2 and plot validation/test F1 vs λ; (c) train with D(θ) alone (attention fit) to check degenerate solutions; (d) control for any other differing hyperparameters between baseline and supervised models.

concerns.title: Sensitivity of S2 Gaussian parameters not explored
concerns.description: S2 depends on Gaussian parameters µ/σ and window size; the claim that S2 yields higher recall vs S1 may hinge on these settings. No parameter sweep or robustness test is presented.
evidence: Section 3.2.2 sets µ=0, σ=1, window=3 but no sensitivity analysis is reported.
Shared_analysis suggests S1 vs S2 precision/recall tradeoff might shift under different µ/σ.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Sweep σ ∈ {0.5,1.0,2.0} and window ∈ {1,3,5} (and possibly µ shifts for asymmetric weighting) and report precision/recall/F1 trends on dev set; include qualitative attention visualizations for representative examples.

concerns.title: FrameNet augmentation pipeline noise unquantified
concerns.description: FrameNet-derived events were automatically processed to obtain arguments and entity mentions via the RPI IE system; the manuscript does not quantify mapping accuracy or labeling noise introduced, leaving ambiguity whether augmentation gains are due to useful signal or spurious effects.
evidence: Section 4.4 describes processing but provides no error analysis or manual spot-checks of the mapped data.
Improvements with FrameNet for ANN-S2 are marginal (0.2 F1), possibly within noise.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide a small manual evaluation (e.g., 100 randomly sampled augmented examples) reporting precision of frame→argument mapping and entity labeling. Report per-class changes and retrain with and without likely-noisy examples to test sensitivity.

concerns.title: Comparability to prior work / reproducibility details missing
concerns.description: Although the ACE split follows prior practice, preprocessing, tokenization, entity-tagging versions, and exact evaluation scripts are not fully specified, making comparisons to prior published results and reproducibility unclear.
evidence: Section 4.1 describes the split but not preprocessing steps or release of code/evaluation scripts.
Comparison table (Table 3) lists prior numbers but different works sometimes use different preprocessing/evaluation conventions.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Release preprocessing and evaluation scripts, random seeds, model code, and exact hyperparameter files. If not possible, clearly document tokenization, named-entity tagger versions, and any normalization steps so others can reproduce the experimental conditions.

concerns.title: Causal claim that unsupervised attention fails due to sparsity is under-tested
concerns.description: The paper attributes ANN's poorer performance to ACE data sparsity and offers FrameNet augmentation as partial evidence, but controlled experiments (learning curves, synthetic data scaling, or capacity adjustments) to isolate data quantity from model formulation are missing.
evidence: Authors reason data sparsity is the cause and cite improvement when adding FrameNet, but no explicit learning-curve or capacity-control ablation is provided.
Shared_analysis recommends learning curve experiments.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Run learning-curve experiments: train ANN and ANN-S2 on increasing fractions of augmented+ACE data to show how attention quality and classification metrics scale. Alternatively, keep data fixed but increase model capacity to check whether architecture underfitting explains ANN behavior.

concerns.title: Attention combination and normalization choices implicit
concerns.description: The model forms final attention α = αw + αe and then uses it to compute cw and ce. No explicit normalization or scaling is discussed for combining two attention sources; interaction effects could bias attention learning.
evidence: Section 3.1.3: 'We combine αw and αe to obtain the final attention vector, α = αw+αe' and then weighted sums cw = Cw α^T, ce = Ce α^T.
No ablation testing alternative combinations (concatenation, weighted sum with learned coefficient) is presented.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Experiment with normalized combinations (e.g., α = softmax(αw + αe) or learn scalar gating between αw and αe) and report whether this stabilizes training or alters performance.

comparable_works.relevance: Structure-based joint event extraction baseline used for comparison in Table 3.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Li's method is structured-prediction/joint and reported lower F1 on ED; differs by using global structured inference rather than supervised attention.
comparable_works.source_trace: Manuscript references Li et al., 2013 in Section 4.3 and Table 3.

comparable_works.relevance: Prior work that used FrameNet to augment ACE; authors reuse their published FrameNet-derived events for augmentation.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similar augmentation idea; current paper focuses on supervising attention with arguments, while Liu et al. focused on leveraging FrameNet corpora to reduce data sparsity.
comparable_works.source_trace: Section 4.4 references Liu et al. (2016a) and uses their data (github link).

comparable_works.relevance: Inspiration for S2 approach using Gaussian spreading around key positions (supervised attention precedent in NMT).
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Mi et al. used supervised attention in neural machine translation; idea of supervising distributional attention around alignments is analogous but applied here to argument positions.
comparable_works.source_trace: Section 3.2.2 cites Mi et al., 2016 as inspiration for Gaussian modeling in S2.

comparable_works.relevance: Strong representation-based ED baseline referenced in Table 3 (reported recall 71.3).
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Different modeling choice (skip-gram CNN) without explicit attention supervision; used as a performance benchmark.
comparable_works.source_trace: Table 3 and Section 4.3 list Skip-CNN as comparison.

comparable_works.relevance: Literature on annotation disagreement and ambiguity relevant to assumptions about argument annotations being reliable supervision targets.
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Does not address ED directly but cautions that single 'gold' annotations may hide ambiguity; relevant interpretive lens for constructing gold attentions.
comparable_works.source_trace: Retrieved literature in reviewer context discusses annotation ambiguity (Aroyo & Welty excerpts).

uncertainty_flags: Statistical testing protocol is underspecified (t-test claim without runs/variance).
Results reported are single point estimates; multiple seeds/standard deviations are not provided.
FrameNet augmentation involves automatic processing and potential label noise that is not quantified.
S1 vs S2 conclusions depend on fixed Gaussian hyperparameters; sensitivity unknown.
Comparability to prior work depends on matching preprocessing/evaluation scripts which are not fully documented.
alternative_interpretations: Performance gains might come partly from hyperparameter tuning (e.g., different λ, dropout) rather than attention supervision per se. Without systematic ablation over λ and training regimes, some gains could be due to better regularization or other training specifics for ANN-S1/S2.

Unsupervised attention's poor performance may be an optimization or architecture issue (e.g., attention parameterization, capacity), not solely data sparsity. Increasing model capacity or changing attention formulation could improve ANN without supervision.

FrameNet augmentation gains might reflect label distribution shifts (more examples of certain event types) rather than generalizable improvement; marginal F1 changes for ANN-S2 could be within measurement noise.

Gold-attention experiments (ANN-Gold1/2) use oracle arguments at test time — their superior performance demonstrates potential upper bound but does not prove learnability of the same attention patterns under noisy/automatic argument detection.
transparency_notes: Manuscript gives explicit model equations, loss terms, and hyperparameters, which facilitates reproduction, but lacks code, preprocessing scripts, seed lists, and repeated-run statistics.
FrameNet augmentation pipeline references an external dataset (Liu et al. 2016a) and uses an external IE tool (RPI Joint IE). The exact versions and parameters of these tools are not listed.
Oracle experiments (ANN-Gold1/2) are valuable for upper-bound analysis but should be clearly labeled as non-deployable/cheating baselines in practice.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The idea of supervising attention is known in other tasks (e.g., Mi et al. 2016 in NMT). Applying supervised attention using event-argument annotations to ED and proposing S1/S2 constructions is a plausible incremental innovation; however, novelty does not guarantee robustness — empirical validation (robustness, reproducibility) is still needed.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If ACE argument annotations are consistent and informative across event types and attention supervision hyperparameters (λ, Gaussian params) are stable, supervised attention will consistently improve ED and generalize to other corpora.

If annotated arguments are noisy or sparse for particular event types, supervised attention could overfit to spurious argument patterns and degrade generalization; success then requires noise-aware mapping or robust loss (e.g., KL, relaxed targets).

If unsupervised attention can be improved via larger training data or alternative attention parameterizations, the relative advantage of supervised attention would shrink, but supervised signals may still speed learning or improve low-data regimes.

novelty_lenses.verdict: Moderately novel in application; conceptually incremental
novelty_lenses.rationale: Supervised attention has prior precedent (e.g., Mi et al., 2016). Using event-argument annotations to supervise attention in ED and offering two pragmatic construction strategies (S1/S2) adapts known ideas to a new task and provides potentially useful engineering contributions.
evidence: Section 3.2.2 cites Mi et al. (2016) and builds S2 on gaussian spreading idea.
Paper frames contribution as architectural/application innovation rather than paradigm shift.
uncertainty_flags: Degree of novelty depends on whether the attention-supervision idea has already been applied to similar IE tasks in closely related literature not retrieved here; absence of direct prior analogs in retrieved set suggests practical novelty but not radical novelty.

novelty_lenses.rationale: Reported gains on ACE 2005 are substantial and could influence ED practice; however, missing robustness tests (repeats, sensitivity, augmentation noise quantification) limit confidence in practical impact.
evidence: ANN-S2 F1=71.7 exceeds listed prior F1 values in Table 3.
ANN-Gold experiments show argument information has strong potential as supervision.
uncertainty_flags: Marginal augmentation gains and under-specified statistical tests weaken the case for broad adoption without further validation.

confidence_interval.rationale: I am moderately confident that (a) supervised attention with argument-derived gold targets improves performance on ACE 2005 relative to the specific unsupervised-attention baseline in this manuscript's experimental setup (evidence: reported point gains), and (b) ANN-S2's F1 advantage over listed prior reported systems is likely but contingent on reproducibility and matched preprocessing. The lower bound reflects uncertainty from missing variance, under-specified t-test protocol, and potential sensitivity to hyperparameters/augmentation noise; the upper bound reflects consistent internal comparisons and plausible empirical effect sizes reported in Tables 3–4.

consensus_findings: Multiple reviewers agree the paper presents a coherent, implementable method: constructing gold attention targets from annotated arguments (S1: argument-only; S2: gaussian-spread) and training an attention-fit auxiliary loss jointly with classification.
Across reported experiments on the stated ACE 2005 split, supervised-attention variants (ANN-S1, ANN-S2) show substantial point improvements over the unsupervised-attention baseline (ANN).

S1 and S2 produce qualitatively different behavior in the reported results: S1 trends toward higher precision, S2 toward higher recall; ANN-S2 attains the highest reported overall F1 in the manuscript's table.
The inclusion of FrameNet-derived examples yields modest increases in recall and slight F1 changes in the reported runs, consistent with a data-quantity/coverage effect.
Authors supplied clear mathematical formulations (attention equations, joint loss) and explicit hyperparameter values, which aids reproducibility in principle.
disagreements: Significance/support for the claim that ANN-S2 strictly outperforms prior published methods: reviewers note the reported point improvement (≈1.0 F1) but disagree about whether the evidence as presented justifies a strong SOTA-type claim because statistical-test details and run variances are missing.

Interpretation of why unsupervised attention underperforms: some reviewers accept data sparsity as a plausible primary cause (supported weakly by FrameNet augmentation effects), while others point to alternative explanations (attention parameterization, optimization, or baseline under-tuning) and ask for controlled isolating experiments.

Appropriateness of technical choices (adding αw and αe; using L2 loss for attention): reviewers differ on whether these are reasonable default choices or methodological weaknesses needing comparative ablations (e.g., normalization, KL loss, gating).
uncertainty_hotspots: Statistical robustness: number of independent runs, random seeds, and variance/confidence intervals for reported P/R/F1 are not reported; the t-test claim is under-specified (no sample size, paired/unpaired status, degrees of freedom).
Causal attribution of unsupervised-attention failure to ACE data sparsity is not isolated experimentally (no learning curves or capacity-controlled ablations).

Sensitivity of the S2 construction (Gaussian µ, σ, window) and of λ balancing between classification and attention loss is untested across ranges; the observed precision/recall tradeoff may depend on these settings.

FrameNet augmentation pipeline: mapping from FrameNet to ACE events, selection of core frame elements, and use of the RPI IE system for entity mentions introduce unquantified noise; its impact on attention supervision and classification is unclear (gains for ANN-S2 are marginal).

Attention composition/normalization and loss choice: the additive combination α = αw + αe and the use of squared-error on attention distributions are presented without comparison to alternatives (gating, normalization, KL/cross-entropy), raising uncertainty about whether design choices are optimal or interacting with reported gains.
model_diversity_effects: Multiple reviewers flagged that supervised attention might be functioning partly as an auxiliary regularizer or inductive bias rather than only as semantic alignment to arguments; this could improve stability or representation learning and thus boost ED metrics even if attention alignment is imperfect.

The ANN baseline's relative weakness could be influenced by architecture/optimization/hyperparameter choices; hence diversity in modeling choices (attention parameterization, capacity, optimization) could reduce or reverse the reported improvement margins.

Augmenting training data (FrameNet) changes model behavior (in reported runs: increased recall). This demonstrates sensitivity of attention learning to dataset composition: additional external examples can compensate for sparsity and alter the supervised vs unsupervised tradeoffs.

Oracle-like models that use gold attention at test time (ANN-Gold1/2) show a sizable upper bound, indicating that argument information is informative; however, practical benefit depends on whether learned attention (ANN-S*) can reliably approximate that oracle under realistic noise conditions.
meta_review.editor_guidance: Preserve the editor's central role in weighing acceptability. If further verification is required before a strong empirical claim is accepted, ask the authors to (1) provide reproducibility artifacts (code, preprocessing/evaluation scripts, random seeds), (2) run and report multiple independent runs (≥5) with mean±std (or bootstrap CIs) and state exact statistical-test procedures, and (3) perform targeted ablations and sensitivity studies (detailed below) to disambiguate attention supervision effects from other factors. Prioritize experiments that directly address the highest epistemic risks: (a) hyperparameter sensitivity (λ, S2 gaussian params), (b) controlled ablation isolating the attention supervision term (sweep λ including 0), (c) learning-curve or capacity-controlled tests to probe the sparsity hypothesis, and (d) small-scale manual audit or noise-quantification of the FrameNet augmentation pipeline. Use those results to reassess comparative claims to prior work, ensuring baseline parity (matched preprocessing and evaluation). The editor should request these artifacts and analyses prior to endorsing strong claims of superiority; if compute or time limits prevent full replication, require the authors to clearly reframe claims as provisional and constrained by the current experimental confirmation level.
meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen evidential claims and reproducibility, provide the following: (1) Code and data-processing scripts (or a runnable container) that produce the ACE split used, including tokenization, sentence-splitting, and any entity-preprocessing, plus the exact evaluation script used; (2) Random seeds and results aggregated across multiple independent runs (report mean and std or bootstrap CIs for P/R/F1); report exact t-test protocol (paired/unpaired, sample size, p-values); (3) Ablations: sweep λ across a grid (e.g., {0, 0.1, 1, 5, 10}) while holding other settings fixed to show dependence of gains on attention supervision; include J-only, D-only experiments or randomized attention-target controls to check for degenerate/regularization effects; (4) Sensitivity study for S2: vary σ and window sizes and report P/R/F1 and whether the precision/recall tradeoff is robust; (5) Normalization/combination and loss-choice ablations: test whether normalizing α after addition, using learned gating between αw and αe, or replacing L2 with KL/cross-entropy changes performance; (6) Recreate key baselines (or re-run them) under your exact preprocessing to ensure fair comparisons; if re-running prior published baselines is infeasible, explicitly document any preprocessing/evaluation differences and temper SOTA claims accordingly; (7) FrameNet augmentation audit: provide a small manual sample-check (e.g., 100 examples) reporting mapping precision/recall and the error modes, and run ablations training with/without RPI-derived entity labels or filtered FN examples to quantify augmentation noise impact; (8) Include qualitative attention visualizations (example heatmaps) showing alignment between learned attention and gold argument positions on dev/test instances and aggregate statistics (e.g., mean attention mass on annotated arguments). These steps will reduce ambiguity about causal mechanisms and strengthen the reproducibility and interpretability of the contribution.
transparency_report: Reported gaps in reproducibility artifacts: no public code, no preprocessing scripts, and no random-seed listing were provided in the reviewed material.

Statistical reporting is insufficient: tables show single point P/R/F1 values without standard deviations or confidence intervals; the t-test claim lacks protocol details (number of runs/samples, paired/unpaired, p-value exactness).

FrameNet augmentation pipeline is described at a high level (use Liu et al. 2016a events, core FEs, RPI IE system for entities) but the exact mapping rules, tool versions, and processing scripts are not included; no noise-quantification (manual or automated) was provided.
Some referenced experimental numbers (e.g., Table 2 gold-attention results) are discussed but not fully tabulated with variance in the excerpts provided to reviewers.
Model-design choices (attention addition αw + αe, L2 loss) are stated but alternatives and normalization details are not fully documented, limiting reproducibility of design intent.
epistemic_limits: The present synthesis cannot adjudicate whether supervised attention is the sole or principal causal driver of the reported gains because critical experimental controls and variance estimates are missing. Without multiple-run statistics and sensitivity/ablation studies, reported point improvements (including the claimed superiority over prior published numbers) may reflect random seed variance, hyperparameter tuning artifacts, preprocessing differences, or regularization effects rather than a replicable methodological advantage. Generalization beyond ACE 2005 (to other IE corpora, domains, or languages) remains untested. The causal claim that unsupervised attention fails primarily due to data sparsity is plausible but not proven here: it remains compatible with alternative explanations (attention parameterization, optimization, baseline under-tuning). Finally, the practical deployability of attention supervision depends on availability and quality of argument annotations or robust automatic argument extraction at test time—this dependency is not quantified, so external validity is limited.

human_facing_meta_review.summary: The manuscript proposes supervising neural attention for event detection (ED) by constructing gold attention vectors from annotated event-arguments (two strategies: S1 argument-only; S2 argument+neighborhood via Gaussian) and adding an L2 attention-fit term to the classification loss. On the reported ACE 2005 split the supervised-attention variants (ANN-S1, ANN-S2) yield sizable point gains over an unsupervised-attention baseline (ANN); ANN-S2 attains the highest reported F1 in the paper's comparison table. Augmenting training with FrameNet-derived events produces modest recall gains. The method is clearly specified and practically implementable, but key robustness, reproducibility, and causal-isolation experiments are missing or underreported (multiple runs/variance, sensitivity to λ and S2 parameters, normalization/combination choices for attentions, and quantification of noise from FrameNet processing).
strengths: Operational clarity: precise definitions for S1 and S2 gold-attention constructions and an explicit joint loss (J' = classification + λ·L2(attention)) make the method straightforward to implement and test.

Empirical signal: within the reported experimental setup on ACE 2005, supervised-attention variants show substantial point improvements over the provided unsupervised-attention baseline and compare favorably to several published systems.

Useful ablation set: inclusion of ANN (unsupervised), ANN-ENT (entity-averaged attention), oracle/gold-attention (ANN-Gold1/2), and supervised variants (ANN-S1/S2) helps trace the potential role of argument information.
Practical augmentation attempt: experimenting with FrameNet-derived events addresses the data-sparsity hypothesis and connects the approach to prior augmentation work.
limitations: Statistical reporting is incomplete: the manuscript reports single-point P/R/F1 numbers and a t-test claim but omits number of independent runs, random seeds, per-run variance or confidence intervals; without repeated runs or bootstrap analyses the robustness of reported gains (including the claimed improvement over prior published numbers) cannot be verified.

Causal attribution not isolated: the claim that unsupervised attention fails primarily due to ACE data sparsity is plausible but not experimentally isolated. Missing experiments include learning curves (vary data size), capacity/attention-parameterization ablations, and controlled λ sweeps to show gains trace specifically to attention supervision rather than other tuning/regularization effects.

Sensitivity and design-choice gaps: S2 depends on Gaussian µ/σ and window hyperparameters and λ balancing; no sensitivity sweeps are reported, and the additive composition α = αw + αe plus the choice of L2 loss for distributions are not compared against alternatives (normalization, gating, KL/cross-entropy).

FrameNet augmentation noise unquantified: the augmentation pipeline uses automatic mappings and an IE tool for entity mentions but provides no audit or error-rate estimate; reported augmentation gains (especially the small +0.2 F1 for ANN-S2) could be within noise introduced by that pipeline.
open_questions: How many independent runs (random seeds) produced the reported test-set numbers? Please provide mean±std (or bootstrap CIs) for P/R/F1 across multiple runs and state exact t-test protocol (paired/unpaired, sample size, p-values).

How sensitive are results to the attention-supervision weight λ and to S2 Gaussian parameters (µ, σ, window)? Please report a sweep (or at least dev-curve) showing how precision/recall/F1 vary with λ and S2 parameters.

Is α = αw + αe normalized before comparison to gold attention α*? Have you compared L2 to distributional losses (KL or cross-entropy) or alternative combinations (learned gating) for combining word and entity attentions?

Can you quantify the noise introduced by FrameNet → ACE mapping and the RPI IE entity labeller? Please report a small manual audit (precision of mapped arguments/entities) and ablation training with/without RPI-labeled entities to show augmentation sensitivity.
consensus_snapshot: Reviewers concur the idea (supervising attention with argument annotations using S1/S2 and a joint loss) is clearly operationalized and practically implementable.

Across provided experiments supervised-attention variants outperform the unsupervised-attention baseline on the reported ACE 2005 split; S1 and S2 show a precision/recall tradeoff (S1 higher precision, S2 higher recall).
FrameNet augmentation produces modest gains consistent with a data-quantity effect, but the augmentation pipeline introduces unquantified noise.
Key reproducibility details (code, preprocessing scripts, seeds) and robustness analyses (multiple runs, λ/S2 sensitivity, normalization/loss alternatives) are missing and recommended.
disagreement_snapshot: Magnitude and credibility of the claimed superiority over prior published methods: some reviewers view the reported ≈1.0 F1 gain as promising but question whether it is robust absent variance reporting and strict parity of preprocessing; others see the point improvement as plausible but conditional on full reproducibility artifacts.

Primary cause of the unsupervised-attention baseline's weakness: some reviewers accept data sparsity as the main cause (supported indirectly by augmentation experiments), while others emphasize alternative explanations (attention parameterization, optimization, or hyperparameter/regularization differences) that require controlled ablations to rule out.
Adequacy of technical choices (additive attention composition and L2 attention loss): reviewers differ on whether these are acceptable defaults or require comparative experiments to justify.
uncertainty_snapshot: High epistemic uncertainty due to missing multiple-run statistics and unspecified t-test protocol—reported gains might reduce under repeated runs or different seeds.

human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary:
The paper introduces a clear, implementable method to supervise attention for event detection using argument annotations (S1: argument-only; S2: Gaussian-smoothed neighborhood). Empirical results on the stated ACE 2005 split report notable point gains for supervised-attention variants over an unsupervised-attention baseline, and ANN-S2 attains the highest F1 in the manuscript's comparison table. The method is practically oriented and connects to prior augmentation work using FrameNet.

Strengths:
- Concrete, reproducible method specification (S1/S2, joint loss) and useful baseline set (ANN, ANN-ENT, ANN-Gold1/2, ANN-S1/S2).
- Measurable empirical gains reported on a standard benchmark (ACE 2005) suggesting attention supervision is a promising inductive bias.
- Consideration of data-sparsity mitigation via FrameNet augmentation connects to prior literature and practical concerns.

Limitations:
- Missing robustness/statistical reporting: no reported mean±std or bootstrap CIs across multiple runs; t-test protocol under-specified. This prevents assessing reliability of point improvements and claimed statistical significance.
- Causal attribution incompletely isolated: absence of λ sweeps, learning-curve/capacity experiments, and controls leaves open alternative explanations (regularization, tuning, attention parametrization) for observed gains.
- Additional methodological concerns: no sensitivity analysis for S2 Gaussian params or for combining/normalizing αw and αe; choice of L2 loss for attention distributions lacks comparison to distributional alternatives.
- FrameNet augmentation pipeline introduces unquantified noise (automatic mapping and IE labeling); marginal gains reported for the best model may be within that noise without further audit.

Open Questions:
- Provide number of runs and random seeds, and report mean±std (or bootstrap CIs). What exactly was the t-test protocol (paired/unpaired; sample size)?
- How do results vary with λ and S2 parameters (σ, window)? Please provide dev/test curves to demonstrate robustness of S1 vs S2 precision/recall trade-offs.
- Is α normalized before comparison to α*? Have you tried KL/cross-entropy or gating alternatives to the additive α composition and L2 loss? If so, report comparative results.
- What is the measured error rate of the FrameNet→ACE mapping and the RPI entity labels? Please provide a small manual audit and ablations with/without those automatic labels.

Transparency:
Manuscript provides equations, model details, and hyperparameters, facilitating reimplementation; however, it lacks code, exact preprocessing/evaluation scripts, random-seed listings, multiple-run statistics, and a documented FrameNet processing pipeline. Oracle (ANN-Gold) experiments should be labeled explicitly as upper-bounds. Providing the requested artifacts and experiments will materially improve reproducibility and reduce interpretive uncertainty.

confidence_interval.rationale: Confidence reflects two axes: (1) conceptual/operational confidence that the method is coherent and implementable (high), and (2) empirical/robustness confidence about the reported gains and comparative SOTA claim (moderate-to-low) because of missing multiple-run statistics, under-specified t-test protocol, sensitivity analyses, and unquantified augmentation noise. The interval expresses moderate overall confidence in the method's promise but substantial epistemic uncertainty about empirical robustness pending the recommended reproducibility and ablation experiments.

Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.
